raw_response:
The strongest mechanism is Ser-codon-island-specific translational fidelity selection: UCN and AGY both encode Ser, but they expose the same intended Ser residue to different rare-error spectra. The selected variable is not speed, tRNA abundance, GC, codon-pair preference, mRNA folding, or ribosome dwell. It is the expression-weighted cost of the wrong amino acids occasionally inserted at that Ser site.
The standard code really does split Ser between the UCN block and the AGY pair; NCBI’s standard code table lists Ser in both the TCN block and AGY positions, using DNA T where RNA would use U. NCBI The graph fact becomes biologically meaningful only if translation errors, mischarging errors, or near-cognate decoding errors are sufficiently local in codon space. If biology does not care about one-step neighborhoods, the missing Ser edge is just a graph curiosity.
For Ser, the two islands have different error neighborhoods. UCN codons are one base away from Pro, Thr, Ala, Phe, Tyr, Cys, Leu, Trp, and, for UCA/UCG, Stop. AGY codons are one base away from Cys, Arg, Gly, Asn, Thr, and Ile. A synonymous UCN↔AGY change therefore preserves the intended Ser but changes the likely identities of mistranslated peptides. That is exactly the kind of mechanism that could make a missing Hamming-1 synonymous bridge matter.
The route is:

$$\text{Ser codon island}
\rightarrow
\text{different near-cognate / mischarging error spectrum}
\rightarrow
\text{different wrong-peptide burden}
\rightarrow
\text{selection at highly expressed or functionally sensitive Ser sites.}$$

The pressure would be something like:

$$\mathrm{Cost}(c,s,\sigma)
=
E_g
\sum_{a\ne Ser}
p(a\mid c,s,\sigma)\,D_s(a),$$

where  $c$  is the Ser codon,  $s$  is the protein site,  $\sigma$  is the condition,  $E_g$  is expression burden,  $p(a\mid c,s,\sigma)$  is the probability that codon  $c$  yields wrong amino acid  $a$ , and  $D_s(a)$  is the site-specific damage caused by that wrong amino acid. The Ser split matters because UCN and AGY change the accessible  $a$ ’s.
The best molecular substrate is conditional fidelity of the Ser decoding channel, not ordinary tRNA supply. UCN and AGY are decoded through different Ser-tRNA routes. Under rich growth they may be effectively equivalent. Under serine limitation, one-carbon stress, oxidative stress, proteostasis stress, altered SerRS behavior, or tRNA-modification stress, those routes could differ in near-cognate rejection, mischarging susceptibility, EF-Tu/EF1A acceptance, or wrong-amino-acid incorporation. There is precedent for environmental perturbations lifting synonymous codon degeneracy: Subramaniam, Pan, and Cluzel reported synthetic-reporter results in E. coli where amino-acid limitation split synonymous codons into robust and sensitive classes, with large protein-output differences, and they reported that the hierarchy was not explained by ordinary codon usage or tRNA abundance. arXiv
But the stronger claim needed here is narrower than that precedent. If the effect is simply “one Ser island has more charged tRNA,” it fails the question. The surviving mechanism must be: at matched charged-tRNA availability, matched wobble controls, matched GC, matched codon-pair context, matched mRNA stability, and matched ribosome dwell, UCN and AGY still yield different peptide-resolved error spectra or different wrong-product costs.
This is also why expression matters. Highly expressed proteins generate many translation events, so rare wrong products become numerous enough for selection to see. Drummond and colleagues framed this class of pressure as selection to reduce the burden of protein misfolding caused by translational missense errors, with pressure increasing with expression level. doi.org The Ser-split version is more specific: synonymous Ser codon choice could tune which rare wrong products are produced at vulnerable Ser sites.
The decisive confounders are harsh.
First, tRNA supply in disguise. Charged Ser-tRNA abundance, tAI, gene copy, isoacceptor abundance, or aminoacylated fraction cannot explain the residual signal. If they do, the mechanism is not independent.
Second, wobble in disguise. UCN and AGY necessarily involve different anticodon systems. A result driven by position-34 pairing, inosine-like breadth, or wobble modification is not the desired mechanism. The signal must be about wrong-product identity or fidelity after wobble effects are removed.
Third, dwell masquerading as fidelity. Lower reporter output, ribosome pausing, collisions, drop-off, or altered elongation speed do not establish this route. The decisive readout is peptide-resolved mistranslation: which wrong amino acids appear at the Ser site, at what rate, under which condition.
Fourth, sequence-composition confounding. UCN and AGY differ in GC, purine/pyrimidine pattern, CpG/UpA potential, RNA motifs, folding, and local codon-pair possibilities. Natural codon enrichment is weak evidence unless these are neutralized.
Fifth, Stop leakage. UCA and UCG are one-step neighbors of Stop codons, whereas UCU/UCC are not. If the apparent effect is only UCA/UCG avoidance, then the mechanism is Stop-adjacency, not a sense-side Ser-island mechanism.
Sixth, protein-position confounding. Ser codon usage can correlate with phosphorylation motifs, catalytic Ser residues, disorder, low-complexity regions, splice enhancers, secretion signals, or gene class. Those may be biologically real, but they are not automatically translation-level codon selection.
So the strongest defensible mechanism is not “UCN is better than AGY” or “AGY is rare.” It is: organisms may use UCN and AGY as two synonymous fidelity modes, choosing the Ser island whose rare mistranslation products are least damaging at highly expressed or functionally constrained Ser residues.
The sharpest next question is: At matched Ser sites and matched expression context, does UCN↔AGY recoding change the peptide-resolved mistranslation spectrum in the direction predicted by the natural codon choice at highly expressed, functionally constrained Ser residues?
